summary.text: Adult cochlear implant user with congenital hearing loss and a learning disability due to maternal rubella, using a MED-EL CONCERTO FLEX28 implant and a contralateral bone-anchored hearing aid. The implanted ear had little auditory stimulation for 35 years before implantation. Electric shock sensation began 3 months and headaches 1 year post switch-on, and FNS when wearing the processor began 5 years post switch-on, after reporting a head strike on the implant side.

On referral, CI-alone sound field auditory thresholds were high at 30 to 40 dB HL and low-frequency sounds were not detected. A CT scan showed partial insertion with 2 extra-cochlear electrodes and an integrity test showed no device failure. Programming attempts to manage FNS, including electrode deactivation, longer pulse durations, mapping changes and a strategy change, did not eliminate FNS.

After a 14-week break and remapping, lower and upper stimulation levels dramatically decreased. FNS recurred at one electrode and pain at two, and the final map with changed pulse durations had no FNS or pain. Levels were later increased for listening comfort, with maplaw changed and electrode 2 deactivated, yet stayed below pre-break levels; further upper-level increases were avoided to prevent recurrent FNS.

The patient used the CI consistently with the bone-anchored hearing aid. Bimodal BKB word scores were 73% at 6 months and 96% at 12 months postbreak, and 21 months after the break the patient described the CI as their long-distance radar. A custom sound diary was used after the break to record symptoms of overstimulation.

summary.text: Adult cochlear implant user diagnosed with hearing loss at 18 months of age after measles, who wore a hearing aid unilaterally from age 4, received a contralateral hearing aid at age 62 and was implanted with a Cochlear CI422 at age 65. Insufficient loudness and compliance issues led to pulse duration increases, and FNS with blepharospasm presented within the first 2 weeks of CI use.

Pulse duration increases up to 150 µs failed to eliminate FNS. One year after switch-on the CI was worn only 3.5 to 5 hours a day, and over the next 3 years loudness could not be achieved without FNS including hemifacial spasms. Headaches and tinnitus occurred only with processor use. Transimpedance matrices were normal and a CT scan ruled out electrode migration.

After a 3-week break, upper and lower stimulation levels decreased and no FNS was observed with a 50 µs pulse duration. Levels had to be increased at 1 and 9 months postbreak for insufficient loudness. FNS recurred nine months after the break as an eye twitch, the patient reported not hearing as well as before, and stimulation levels were increased again.

Performance and device wearing time remained limited, with average usage 3.6 h/d before the break and 3.7 h after it. A§E scores were 60% before the break and 55% to 65% after it. Stimulation levels remained below prebreak levels in follow-up and FNS was decreased or eliminated.

summary.text: Adult with hearing loss associated with dominant optic atrophy due to OPA1 mutation, diagnosed at 6 years of age, who was implanted in adulthood with an Advanced Bionics device. Within 1 year after implantation they reported intermittent sound, pain, facial twitching, poor battery life and electric shock, and were reimplanted with a Cochlear CI24RE CA device. FNS onset is listed at switch-on.

After reimplantation loudness was low despite high stimulation levels, the dynamic range was narrow, and severe FNS and pain occurred; sound quality was beeping or buzzing and audibility decreased over time, with deterioration in vision and balance. An integrity test showed no device failure, and mapping modifications were unsuccessful. An auditory brainstem implant was offered and declined.

The patient had several periods of nonuse due to lack of sound perception and pain or FNS. After a spontaneous long break between 2 sessions, stimulation levels decreased, then rose 2 months later without reaching prebreak levels. Ten-year follow-up showed high, increasing stimulation levels with insufficient loudness and clarity and persistent pain and FNS; the break was not sufficient for managing FNS.

summary.text: Adult with a history of meningitis who received a cochlear implant at age 48 years. Pain was reported 10 years after switch-on and FNS 3 years later, 13 years post switch-on. FNS was severe, manifesting as blepharospasm, pain and electric shock that persisted even without the processor switched on, though much worse when worn.

Pulse duration increases up to 150 µs overall and 400 µs for FNS-inducing electrodes, different grounding configurations and deactivation of up to 9 electrodes failed to reduce FNS and significantly reduced subjectively reported auditory performance. BKB scores failed to return to pre-FNS levels. Table 1 lists 16 electrodes leading to FNS before the break.

After a 1-week break, FNS thresholds decreased slightly for some electrodes and were unchanged for others, 16 electrodes still led to FNS, and most electrodes could not reach a comfortably loud rating below the FNS threshold. No programming changes were made and the same map was used. The authors suggested the break was not effective; the patient was treated by reimplantation with an Oticon Medical device.
